topic: The American Civil War was a conflict between the Union and the Confederate States that ended slavery and laid the groundwork for ongoing economic and social disparities among Black Americans.

plan.question: How did a nation survive its own division?

cast.name: Robert E. Lee
cast.role: Commander of the Army of Northern Virginia

chapters.title: A Nation Torn Apart
beats: A nation torn apart by irreconcilable differences. Two governments claiming authority over the same land and people. A conflict that would claim hundreds of thousands of lives and reshape a continent. The United States faced its greatest test as brother fought against brother. Four million enslaved people awaited their fate. The world watched as the experiment in democracy hung in the balance. Economic systems clashed, cultures collided, and families were divided. When the smoke cleared, one nation would remain, but at what cost? How did America survive its own division?

chapters.title: Leaders Divided
beats: In Washington, Abraham Lincoln led the United States, determined to preserve the Union at all costs. Opposite him stood Jefferson Davis, president of the newly formed Confederate States, fighting for independence and the right to maintain their economic system. In Richmond, Davis commanded a government built on the foundation of states' rights and slavery. Robert E. Lee, commander of the Army of Northern Virginia, pledged his loyalty to Virginia despite his personal opposition to secession. Ulysses S. Grant, leading Union armies, emerged as Lincoln's most trusted general, willing to pay any price for victory. William Tecumseh Sherman, conducting devastating campaigns through the South, believed total war was necessary to break the Confederacy's will. Washington, D.C. served as the Union capital, symbolizing the federal government's authority. Richmond housed the Confederate government, representing their breakaway nation. Gettysburg witnessed the bloodiest battle of the war, Atlanta became the focus of Sherman's campaign, and Appomattox Court House marked the war's end where surrender terms were negotiated.

chapters.title: The First Crack
beats: December 1860: South Carolina voted to secede from the Union, setting a dangerous precedent. Lincoln, newly inaugurated in March, faced a country already fracturing before he could fully establish his authority. Davis, having formed the Confederate States in February, prepared for conflict while maintaining a facade of peaceful intentions. April 1861: Confederate forces opened fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston, a federal installation in Southern territory. The attack that began with 4,000 shells fired at the fort transformed political disagreement into open warfare. Lincoln, responding to the attack, called on states to field 75,000 militiamen for 90 days, viewing the rebellion as a temporary disturbance that required a limited response. Virginia's secession on April 17 brought the war closer to Washington and gave the Confederacy its most valuable military asset in Robert E. Lee. The first battle at Bull Run in July shattered illusions of a quick, bloodless conflict, as thousands of men fell in the first major engagement.

chapters.title: The Long Road Ahead
beats: After the First Battle of Bull Run revealed the war's true scale, Lincoln realized this would require more than 90 days of service. May 1861: Lincoln called for an additional 42,000 volunteers for three years, acknowledging the conflict would be long and arduous. Davis, seeing the Union's determination to fight, accelerated Confederate mobilization while attempting to secure foreign recognition. Lee, now commanding Virginia's forces, began organizing defenses around Richmond, knowing the capital would be the Union's primary target. September 1861: Lincoln took drastic measures to secure Maryland, seizing prominent figures including one-third of the Maryland General Assembly to prevent the state from joining the Confederacy. November 1861: George B. McClellan became general-in-chief of Union armies, promising to organize the inexperienced Northern forces into an effective fighting machine. Davis struggled to maintain Confederate unity as border states like Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina joined the secession, stretching the Confederacy's resources and complicating its defense strategy. The first year of the war established patterns that would define the conflict: the Union's numerical advantage versus the Confederacy's defensive advantages, the political resolve on both sides, and the growing realization that this would be a war of unprecedented bloodshed.

chapters.title: A New Purpose
beats: The Emancipation Proclamation marked the war's turning point. Lincoln's decision fundamentally altered the conflict's purpose, shifting from merely preserving the Union to ending slavery. By making abolition a war aim, Lincoln prevented European powers from recognizing the Confederacy, as European nations had abolished slavery decades earlier. The proclamation also allowed African Americans to enlist in the union army, adding nearly 180,000 soldiers to Northern forces. Davis, recognizing the proclamation's impact, intensified efforts to secure foreign recognition while doubling down on slavery as essential to Confederate identity. Lee, understanding the strategic implications, prepared for an invasion of Pennsylvania to pressure Lincoln to negotiate peace and potentially win European support. The Union's acceptance of emancipation as a war aim committed the nation to a new path, one that would redefine American society and ensure the war's outcome would include the destruction of slavery.
